newsitem.title: USA: Browner defends air plan to hostile congressmen.
newsitem.headline: Browner defends air plan to hostile congressmen.

text.p: Just days before sending her final recommendation to the White House on clean air rules, Environmental Protection Agency Administrator Carol Browner Thursday said the public supports cleaner air standards.

"Based on our reading of the best available science, I have proposed new standards for particulate matter and ozone (soot and smog) that I believe are required to protect the health of the American people," Browner told a House panel.

Republicans, and some Democrats, on the House Commerce and Oversight and Investigation subcommittees at the joint hearing were openly hostile to the proposal, which industry groups say will cost them billions of dollars.

A growing number of House and Senate Democrats urged the Clinton administration to delay the rule, saying that the scientific community is split on the need for tougher standards and that it may cause a backlash against pollution laws.
But Browner said public comments the agency received "show a great deal of support for these proposals."

She also said although she had not made a final decision on whether to strengthen the standards, "I can ... say that we have not found anything in the public comments that causes us to question the science upon which these proposals are based."
Browner said she hoped to submit the agency's final proposal to the White House Office of Management and Budget around May 20, but said it might be later than that.
The administration is to announce a final rule in July. Under a law passed last year, Congress then has a chance to vote on the final rule.

Asked by reporters whether she was concerned by the Democratic opposition to her proposal, Browner said, "The law didn't say to me to consider what may or may not happen down the road. The law said to set a public health standard based on the best available science."
Browner also disputed that pollution control measures to meet the new standards would require changes in peoples' lifestyles, such as limiting barbeques and fireplaces.
Reducing emissions from big utility power plants would be the major step to bring many areas into compliance, she said.
